scenes.visual: Title 'How Barriers Between Species Grow' over pink and red flower silhouettes.

scenes.tts: Two monkeyflowers can be crossed by hand to give hybrid seed. One is pink, visited mostly by bumblebees. The other is red, visited mostly by hummingbirds. Yet in the wild, almost no genes pass between them. That is what makes them two species. Speciation is the evolution of barriers that cut gene flow between populations. And for these flowers, the barriers grew mostly out of adapting to different places and different pollinators.

scenes.visual: Pink and red flowers with a hand-cross arrow and hybrid seed; a gene-flow band between them thins almost to nothing; the words 'barriers to gene flow' appear in the gap.

scenes.tts: A reproductive barrier is anything that reduces gene flow. Barriers are sorted by when they act. Where the plants grow, and which pollinators visit them, act before the zygote, the fertilized egg. Low hybrid fertility acts after. No single barrier here is complete, and most of the isolation comes before any hybrid forms.

scenes.visual: Three barrier chips (habitat, pollinator, hybrid fertility) sorted either side of a dashed zygote line; the before-zygote side glows larger.

scenes.tts: These barriers were not built on purpose. One species is adapted to lower elevations, the other to higher ones. One flower suits bumblebees, the other suits hummingbirds. So the plants rarely meet, and a pollinator carries little pollen between them. Isolation is a side effect of adaptation. This is ecological speciation, driven by divergent selection.

scenes.visual: A mountain slope: red flowers low, pink flowers high; a hummingbird and a bumblebee each stay on their own flower; the habitat and pollinator chips from s02 snap onto the slope.

scenes.tts: How do we know selection did this, and not chance? Lakes in British Columbia each hold a bottom-feeding and an open-water stickleback, and each lake's pair seems to have arisen on its own. In mating trials, fish of different forms rarely mated, but same-form fish from different lakes mated readily. Isolation followed ecology, lake after lake.

scenes.visual: Three lake outlines, each with a benthic and a limnetic fish; cross-lake same-form pairs join with green links, different-form pairs get red breaks.

scenes.tts: Barriers act in sequence. Each one can only block the gene flow that earlier barriers left behind. So, if they act independently, the fractions that get through multiply, and total isolation is one minus their product. Never just add the raw strengths. Their sum can be more than one, which means nothing as a fraction of gene flow.

scenes.visual: A gene-flow band passes three gates and narrows at each; the formula 1 - (1 - RI1) x (1 - RI2) x (1 - RI3) appears; a raw sum is struck out.

scenes.tts: Where speciation happens is a separate question from how. A sea or a mountain range can split a population, which is allopatric speciation. Or forms can diverge in one place, which is sympatric speciation. Living together today does not prove a sympatric start. For crater-lake cichlids in Nicaragua, genome-wide models supported divergence inside the lake, with some genes arriving from outside.

scenes.tts: There is also a faster route. In plants especially, a hybrid can double its whole genome. The new polyploid lineage is partly isolated from its parents in a single generation. Either way, the result is the same. Barriers cut gene flow, and a new lineage evolves on its own.
